[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday thinking pictures a variable as a box that holds the thing itself. That is true for int, double, char and boolean; an array variable holds only the address of the array, which is stored elsewhere.
[1] misconception (M) -> VariablesHoldObjects: wrong rule: A reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference. Right rule: An array variable stores a reference (the memory address) to the array, not the elements.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> VariablesHoldObjects: Applies the model unevenly: treats int x = y as copying a value (correct) but also treats b = a for arrays as copying all the elements. (here mixing in: "a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference")
[3] misconception (M) -> StringIsPrimitive: wrong rule: String is a primitive type like int. Right rule: Java has eight primitive types; String is not one of them, and a String variable holds a reference.

[0] names_the_element (N): Primitive versus reference variable: the first holds its value, the second holds the address of an object.
[1] states_the_rule (S): When you declare a variable of a primitive type, Java reserves memory that stores its value. An array variable stores a reference to the array: Java treats the array name as a variable whose value is the memory address of the array.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: x = y copies the value of y into x; b = a copies the address in a into b. In both cases the right side is evaluated first and its value stored, but the value of an array variable is an address.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: after int y = x; y++, x is unchanged; after int[] b = a; b[0]++, a[0] has changed too, because a and b refer to the same array.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: assigning to a primitive variable changes only that variable; assigning to an element through a reference changes the array that every reference to it sees.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The eight primitive types are the ones whose variables hold the value itself.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): An array variable is the standard example of a reference: its value is the memory address of the array.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: the model predicts when an assignment shares data (arrays, Strings) and when it copies it (primitives), which decides when a copy is needed.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> VariablesHoldObjects: Conservation: changing a primitive copy never affects the original; changing an array through any reference affects every alias.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Draw a memory diagram (value in a box for primitives, an arrow to the array for references) whenever code assigns or compares arrays.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: == on references compares addresses. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: two arrays with the same elements are compared with == and found unequal (or two Strings with the same text)
wrong: s == t is true whenever the two Strings contain the same text. | right: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.
wrong: String is a primitive type like int. | right: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).
wrong: == compares contents (the String == bug) | right: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.
wrong: String is a primitive type like int. | right: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).
wrong: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference | right: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.
wrong: s == t is true whenever the two Strings contain the same text. | right: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.
wrong: String is a primitive type like int. | right: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).
wrong: A String or array variable contains the whole object inside it. | right: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.
An array variable stores the memory address of the array, not its elements.
A variable of a primitive type stores the value itself in its own memory.
